# The Lumen Standard Library

Every module here ships with the language and needs no installation.

## The prelude

These are available in every file with no import at all. A binding of your own
with the same name always shadows the prelude one.

Everything else lives in a `std/*` module.

## Conventions

Three rules hold across the whole library, and knowing them saves reading every
signature:

1. **The subject comes first.** `map(xs, f)`, `split(s, sep)`, `get(m, key)`.
   This is what makes `xs |> filter(pred) |> map(f) |> sum()` read left to right.
2. **Nothing mutates unless its name says so.** `push` and `pop` change their
   list in place; `set`, `remove`, `merge`, `sort` and `reverse` all return new
   values. The checker knows which is which: `xs.sort()` on a line of its own
   is `TY010`, a statement that does nothing, while `xs.push(1)` is not.
3. **Fallible operations return a `Result`; absence returns an `Option`.**
   Reading a file returns `Result`. Looking up a key returns `Option`. Neither
   ever raises for an ordinary failure.

## Notes on particular modules

### Numbers as text

`fixed(n, places)` gives a number as text with exactly that many decimals:
`fixed(4.5, 2)` is `"4.50"`, which `round(n * 100) / 100` cannot produce
because the trailing zero is not part of the number. It is what a column of
money or percentages needs, and it is in the prelude.

For width, compose: `fixed(x, 2).padStart(8)`.

### `std/core`

`args()` is the arguments after your script's name, and nothing else — the script
path is never in it. It is the same list however the program was started, so
`lumen run app.lm --verbose` and `lumen app.lm --verbose` both give
`["--verbose"]`. Anything the CLI would otherwise read as its own option is
still the program's once a filename has been seen.

`now()` is milliseconds since 1970. Under the test harness it is `0`, so a
golden file cannot depend on the clock.

`clone(value)` is a **deep** copy: nested lists, maps, structs and enum payloads
are copied too, so nothing in the copy is shared with the original. Two things
follow, and both are deliberate. A value that appears twice inside another stays
one value in the copy rather than becoming two — copying a value should not change
its shape. And a value that contains itself can be cloned, giving a copy with its
own cycle. Numbers, strings and functions are returned as they are, having nothing
to copy.

**A group key must be a faithful identity.** `groupBy` and `map.invert` both
turn a value into a `Map` key, and a `Map`'s keys are text — so the value has to
print to something that tells two of them apart. `Str`, `Num` and `Bool` do.
A `Map`, a `List` or a struct does not, and both functions were wrong in both
directions at once: `{city: "Oslo", zone: 1}` and `{zone: 1, city: "Oslo"}` are
`==` and print differently, so they became *two* groups; `1` and `"1"` are not
`==` and both print `1`, so they became *one*, and `invert` silently dropped an
entry.

Neither is exotic — data from a CSV is all `Str` and data from JSON is mixed, so
an `id` that is sometimes `7` and sometimes `"7"` is ordinary. Both are refused
now, with the reason, the same way `std/csv` refuses a duplicate column: one of
the two would silently win and which one is not something a reader could
predict. Two values of the *same* type landing on the same text really are one
key, which is what `groupBy` is for and what `invert`'s "the last one wins"
means.

### `std/set`

A set is a `List` with no duplicates — there is no separate `Set` type — so every
`std/list` function still works on one and `print` shows it as you would write
it. Each function keeps the order of its first argument, because a program that
prints a set has to print it in *some* order and the order you built it in is the
only one that is stable across runs.

Membership is exactly `==`, including for nested values: two structs with equal
fields are one element, and so are two maps with the same entries inserted in a
different order.

`union`, `intersection`, `difference`, `symmetricDifference`, `isSubset` and
`equals` index one side and walk the other, so they are linear rather than
quadratic — which is why the module exists, since the same thing written with
`filter` and `contains` is quadratic and quietly so. `has`, `add` and `remove`
answer one question and still have to build that index, so they are linear too:
no worse than `contains`, and no better.

`equals` answers the question `==` cannot. `[1, 2] == [2, 1]` is `false`, which
is right for lists; `equals([1, 2], [2, 1])` is `true`.

### `std/time`

An instant is a `Num` of milliseconds since 1970 — the same number `now()`
returns. There is no date type, so `later - earlier` is the elapsed
milliseconds, `<` compares two instants, and `sorted()` sorts a list of them
without this module being involved.

**Everything is UTC.** That is a decision, not a shortcut. Real local time needs
time-zone names, which needs the IANA database — a dependency that changes
several times a year — and a program that followed the machine's zone would print
different things on different computers, which would make a golden test file or a
date-stamped filename depend on where it ran.

`offsetMinutes(instant)` is the one door to local time: what this machine
believes its offset from UTC is *at that instant*, so daylight saving is
accounted for. Add it to shift an instant for display, and the assumption is
visible where it is made:

```lumen
let local = t + offsetMinutes(t) * 60000
print("filed at ${time(local)} local")
```

`format` replaces `YYYY MM DD hh mm ss SSS` and leaves every other character
alone. There is nothing to escape, which is the trade: a template cannot contain
a literal `MM`, and in exchange there are no rules to get wrong.

`plus` shifts by days, hours, minutes and seconds only. Months and years are not
fixed lengths, so "one month later" has no single answer — `fromParts` with
`month + 1` says which one you meant, and rolls over for you (month 13 is January
of the next year; day 0 is the last day of the month before).

`parseIso` reads text with no zone as UTC, for the same reason the rest of the
module is UTC: guessing would make the same input mean different instants on
different machines.

### `std/list` and `std/map`

`first`, `last`, `at`, `find` and `map.get` return an `Option`, so "there wasn't
one" is a value you handle rather than a `nil` you forget about.

`len` exists both in the prelude and in these modules. Importing the module's
version shadows the prelude's; either works on the right type.

### `std/json`

`parse` returns `Result`, and its error says **where**:

```text
invalid JSON at line 3, column 29: a trailing comma: JSON has no comma before `]`
invalid JSON at line 1, column 2: the key `name` needs double quotes around it
invalid JSON at line 1, column 1: `tru` is not a value JSON knows — did you mean `true`?
```

Both the wording and the position are Lumen's own. The wording, because V8
rewrites its JSON error text between Node releases and a Lumen program's output
must not depend on which Node happens to be running it. The position, because
the alternative was the four words "invalid JSON", which is not something
anybody can act on about a file somebody else exported — and every other
diagnostic in this language says where.

That means a second scan of the text, beside the host's parser, and it runs
**only** after the host has already refused the document. So it can never affect
a document that parses, and the worst a bug in it could do is produce a vaguer
message. A test checks the two against each other over 200,000 generated
documents: the locator finds a problem exactly when `JSON.parse` refuses the
text.

`stringify` renders structs as objects and enums as their variant name (or
`{variant, values}` when they carry a payload).

**A number JSON cannot write is refused.** `Infinity` and `NaN` are ordinary
Lumen values — the spec says overflow to `Infinity` is not an error — and JSON
has no way to spell either. `JSON.stringify` writes `null` for both without a
word, which is the worst possible substitute: `null` is how JSON spells
*absent*, so an overflowed total does not merely lose its magnitude, it comes
back looking like a field nobody filled in. It is a panic naming the path, like
a cycle and like a function.

A value that contains itself cannot be written as JSON at all — there is no
syntax for "the value we are already inside" — so `stringify` refuses and names
where the cycle closes. It is the only operation that has to: `print`, `==`,
`clone` and set membership all handle a cyclic value.

`Option` is the exception: `Some(v)` becomes `v` and `None` becomes `null`. An
optional field is the commonest thing in a JSON document and JSON already spells
it, so `{"nickname": "addy"}` rather than
`{"nickname": {"variant": "Some", "values": ["addy"]}}`. `Result` keeps the
tagged form — there is no agreed JSON shape for "succeeded or failed", and
unlike `Option` both of its arms carry something the reader has to tell apart.
The cost is that `Some(nil)` and `None` both become `null`, which is JSON's
limit rather than a choice: there is no second null to map the other one to.

**A character is a code point.** `len`, `slice`, `chars`, `reverse`, `indexOf`,
`padStart`, `padEnd` and `center` all count the same thing, which is the only
property that makes them usable together: `slice(s, indexOf(s, ":"))` has to cut
where `indexOf` pointed, and `padEnd(s, 28)` has to produce something `len`
calls 28 or a table column is short by one for every row whose text has an emoji
in it. JavaScript counts UTF-16 units, where an emoji is two; every function
here that takes or gives a position or a width converts.

It is not a grapheme cluster, and does not claim to be: `reverse` of an `e`
followed by a combining acute still moves the accent, and there is no
dependency-free way to do better. Code points are where the line is drawn, and
everything here draws it in the same place.

### `std/web`

A handler is any function from a request to a response.

`router` builds one from a list of `route`s, so a site does not need a chain of
`if req.path == ...`:

```lumen
let app = router([
  route("GET", "/", fn(req) { html("<h1>home</h1>") }),
  route("GET", "/post/new", fn(req) { html(newPostForm()) }),
  route("GET", "/post/:slug", fn(req) { postPage(req.params.slug) }),
  route("GET POST", "/contact", fn(req) { contact(req) }),
  route("GET", "/static/*path", fn(req) { file(req.params.path, root: "public") }),
])
serve(handler: app, port: 3000)
```

A pattern is literal segments plus two kinds of hole: `:name` matches one
segment, and `*name` matches the rest of the path. What they capture arrives in
`req.params`, so every handler takes one argument whether it has parameters or
not, decoded — `/post/a%20b` gives `a b`. A method may name several verbs
separated by spaces.

Routes are tried in order, so the specific one goes first: `/post/new` above
`/post/:slug`, or the second answers for both.

Two things it gets right that a hand-written chain usually does not:

- A request whose **path matches but whose method does not** gets **405** with an
  `allow` header naming the methods that would have worked — not 404. A client
  cannot otherwise tell a wrong URL from a wrong verb.
- **A trailing slash is not a different route.** `/about` and `/about/` are one
  path, because links and browsers add and remove that slash freely.

`notFound:` replaces the 404, and takes the request so it can say what was
missing.

A **request** is a `Map` with `method`, `path`, `query`, `headers` and `body`.
A **response** is a `Map` with `status`, `headers` and `body` — the helpers build
one for you, and returning a bare `Str` is treated as HTML.

```lumen
import { serve, page, json, notFound, escape } from "std/web"

fn handle(req) {
  if req.path == "/" {
    page(title: "Home", body: "<h1>hello</h1>")
  } else if req.path == "/health" {
    json({ ok: true })
  } else {
    notFound("<p>no ${escape(req.path)}</p>")
  }
}

serve(handler: handle, port: 3000)
```

`serve` never returns — a web server that exited on its own would be a bug.

**`escape` for text, `url` for a link.** `escape` turns `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and
`'` into entities, which is exactly right for the body of an element and for a
quoted attribute value, and is what almost every use needs. It is the wrong tool
for an `href`, and this page used to say otherwise:

```text
<a href="${escape(link)}">   with link = javascript:alert(document.cookie)
→ <a href="javascript:alert(document.cookie)">
```

The advice followed exactly, and a working cross-site script — because there is
nothing in `javascript:alert(1)` to escape. Escaping answers *"could this text
break out of where I am putting it"*; a link needs *"does this text tell the
browser to run something"*, which is a different question. `url(link)` answers
that one: a scheme that is not `http`, `https`, `mailto` or `tel` becomes
`about:blank`, and the result is escaped for the attribute as well, so it is one
call rather than two. The scheme is read the way a browser reads it, with
leading whitespace and control characters stripped first, because
`java\tscript:alert(1)` is `javascript:` to a browser and was not to a naive
check.

Neither is the tool for text inside a `<script>` block — nothing here is. Put
the value in a `data-` attribute and read it from there, or send it as JSON.
A relative link needs no scheme and is left alone, as is a protocol-relative
`//host/path`: that navigates rather than executing, so whether to allow it is
an open-redirect question for the program to answer.

`form(req)` reads the fields a form submitted, whichever way the page sent
them: the query string for `method="get"`, the urlencoded body for
`method="post"`. A handler that uses it does not have to know which, and a
request carrying anything else — JSON, a file upload — comes back empty with
`req.body` still there to parse.

**`formAll(req)` when a name can repeat.** A `Map` holds one value per key, so
`?tag=a&tag=b&tag=c` reaches `form` as `{tag: "c"}` — and a checkbox group and a
`<select multiple>` are exactly that shape, and are ordinary HTML. `formAll`
answers with a list per field instead, including for the fields that appeared
once, because a type that changes with the input is worse than one that is
always the same. Both read the same request; only what they do with a repeat
differs. `req.search` carries the query as it arrived, which is where `formAll`
recovers the repeats `req.query` has already dropped.

```lumen
fn handle(req) {
  let fields = form(req)
  let name = if fields.has("name") { fields["name"] } else { "world" }
  page(title: "Hello", body: "<p>hello, ${escape(name)}</p>")
}
```

`file(path, root)` serves a file from a directory, or a 404 if it is not there.
The content type comes from the extension, a directory resolves to its
`index.html`, and binary files come back byte for byte.

```lumen
fn handle(req) {
  if req.path.startsWith("/static/") { file(req.path.slice(7), root: "public") }
  else { page(title: "Home", body: "<h1>hello</h1>") }
}
```

**`root` is a boundary, not a suggestion.** The obvious thing to write —
`file(req.path, root: "public")` — is also the classic way to hand out
`/etc/passwd`, because `public/../../etc/passwd` is a perfectly good path and
`%2e%2e%2f` arrives looking innocent. `file` decodes the path first, resolves
it, and then compares the result against the resolved root; anything outside is
a 404. Not a 403: telling an attacker which of "no such file" and "not yours to
ask for" happened is itself information.

The comparison happens **twice**, because once is not enough. The first is on
the path as written; the second is on what the filesystem really has, once every
symlink is followed. A link inside the root pointing anywhere at all resolves to
something that *looks* inside it, and nothing about the request has to be
strange for one to be there — an upload directory, a linked build artefact, a
`node_modules` somebody symlinked. A link that stays inside the root still
works, since `current -> releases/v3` is how deployments are arranged.

**A name beginning with a dot is not served.** `.env` and `.git/config` are the
most-exploited misconfiguration on the web, and `file`'s default `root` is `"."`
— the directory the program is running in, which in a checkout holds both.
`.well-known` is the one exception, and it is not optional: it is where a
certificate authority looks to prove the site is yours, so blocking it would
break HTTPS rather than protect anything.

`isServer()` says whether the file was started with `lumen serve` or with
`lumen run`. Branching on it lets one file be both a site and a script — serve
the routes when asked to serve, and print what they return when asked to run —
which is how a website stays testable from the command line.

### `std/ai`

Which provider runs is decided in this order:

1. an explicit `provider:` argument
2. `LUMEN_AI_PROVIDER` in the environment
3. `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, then `OPENAI_API_KEY`
4. otherwise the built-in `mock` provider

An explicit argument counts only when it **names** something. `provider: ""`
and `provider: nil` do not, so step 1 does not apply to them and step 2 does —
which is what `chat(prompt, provider: config.getOr("provider", ""))` needs to be
safe. It was not: the empty string used to skip the environment entirely and
fall through to step 3, so an empty default in a config file silently cancelled
`LUMEN_AI_PROVIDER=mock` and sent the prompt to the real API with the real key.

The `mock` provider is deliberate, not a stub: it makes examples, tests and CI
run with no key, no network and a deterministic answer. Real credentials are
strictly opt-in.

Every call returns a `Result`, so a rate limit or a network failure is a value
you handle rather than a crash.

```lumen
import { chat, converse, message, provider } from "std/ai"

match chat(prompt: "Explain recursion in one sentence.", maxTokens: 200) {
  Ok(reply) => print(reply),
  Err(why)  => print("failed: ${why}"),
}
```

`model` defaults to `claude-opus-5` for Anthropic and `gpt-4o-mini` for OpenAI,
and `LUMEN_AI_MODEL` overrides both.

`LUMEN_AI_MOCK_REPLY` makes the mock provider say exactly one thing, whatever
it is asked. A program that asks the model for JSON and then parses it has two
outcomes worth testing — the reply parsed, and the reply did not — and without
this only the second is reachable with no key. It is a testing affordance, not
a model: the mock never reads the prompt to decide what to say.

```bash
lumen run examples/triage.lm                                  # the reply is prose
LUMEN_AI_MOCK_REPLY='{"category":"bug","urgency":5}' \
  lumen run examples/triage.lm                                # the reply parses
```

A reply is text, always. Ask for JSON and you will still sometimes get prose,
an apology, or JSON inside a code fence — so check the shape rather than
trusting it, and have something to do when it is wrong.
`examples/triage.lm` is that program written out, retries included.

### `std/option` and `std/result`

**`or` is a method and nothing else.** `maybe.or(fallback)` works; `or(maybe,
fallback)` is a syntax error, because `or` in that position is the logical
operator and `a or (b)` cannot be told from `or(a, b)`. It is the one export in
the library whose three spellings are not one expression, and it keeps the name
because `maybe.or(fallback)` is how every language with an `Option` says it —
the reading that matters is the one that works. A test holds the rest of the
library to the rule, so a future `and` or `in` is caught before it ships.

`match` is the honest way to handle absence or failure and will always be
there. But a great many uses of an Option or a Result are one of three shapes —
turn the value into another value, supply a default, ask which one you have —
and writing each of those as a two-armed `match` buries the interesting line in
ceremony:

```lumen
match find(notes, id) { Some(n) => n.title, None => "(none)" }
find(notes, id).map(title).unwrapOr("(none)")
```

Both take their subject first, so every function is also a method.

| Option | Result |
|---|---|
| `isSome` `isNone` | `isOk` `isErr` |
| `unwrapOr(fallback)` | `unwrapOr(fallback)` |
| `map(f)` `andThen(f)` | `map(f)` `andThen(f)` `mapErr(f)` |
| `filter(p)` `or(other)` | `ok()` `err()` — as an Option |
| `okOr(error)` `toList()` | |

`andThen` is for a function that returns an Option or Result of its own, so
nothing is wrapped twice; a function that returns something else is an error
rather than a silent double wrap. `mapErr` is what adds context to a failure as
it travels up: `read(path).mapErr(fn(e) { "loading config: ${e}" })`.

`or` is a keyword, and callable here only because a keyword after a `.` can be
nothing but a name (spec §1.4).

### `std/fs` and `std/http`

Error text belongs to Lumen, not to the host — and a test asks that of the
whole library at once rather than function by function, because it was a rule
kept by hand until `std/process` broke it. It calls every export with an
argument of the wrong shape and with the awkward values (an empty string, a
zero, an empty list), and fails if the answer contains a word only the host
would use. The boundary values are the half that matters: `run("")` was what
produced a raw `TypeError`, and no wrong *type* goes anywhere near it. Node's own filesystem messages
name an errno, a syscall and a quoting style that differ between platforms and
versions, so `std/fs` maps the stable part — the error code — to a sentence of
its own: `cannot read \`config.json\`: no such file or directory`. A code with
no sentence yet keeps the code rather than hiding it behind something vague.
`std/http` names the request that failed, since "fetch failed" on its own says
nothing when several are in flight — and it also names what is wrong with a URL
it will not fetch. The host does not: `file://…` answered "not implemented...
yet...", and `blob:…` answered "invalid method" for a GET. Only the scheme is
wrong, so the scheme is what the message says. `std/ai` said the bare "fetch
failed" this paragraph singles out until it was told to do the same.

**Every `Set-Cookie` is reachable, in `cookies`.** It is the one header the
Fetch API deliberately does not combine — a cookie value can contain a comma
(`Expires=Wed, 09 Jun 2021`), so a joined form could not be split back — which
meant `headers["set-cookie"]` held only one of them. A login response setting a
session cookie and a CSRF token gave up one of the two, silently, and reading
`set-cookie` is very nearly the only reason to look at a response's headers at
all. `response.cookies` is a `List<Str>` of all of them, in order; every other
repeated header is still combined in `headers`, which is correct and is why this
is a new field rather than a change to an old one.

**A header value must be a `Str` or a `Num`.** Anything else used to go out as
an *empty* header, which is the one answer that is silently wrong:
`headers: { authorization: token }` where `token` came back `nil` — a config
value that was not there — put `authorization:` on the wire with nothing after
it, and the server's 401 then sent the reader hunting for a token problem rather
than a nil.

This is the same reason `std/json` writes its own `invalid JSON at line 3,
column 29: ...` rather than passing through V8's parser message: a Lumen program
should print the same thing wherever it runs. Refusing the host's *wording* is
not a reason to refuse to say where, so the position is worked out here.

Both are `Result`-returning throughout. An HTTP response with a non-2xx status
is still `Ok` — the *request* succeeded; check `status` to decide what it means.

`std/time.parseIso` overrides the host for the same reason. Node validates a
month and rejects `2024-13-01`, and then accepts `2024-02-30` and answers March
1st — so a date read out of somebody's file moves by a day and nothing says so.
That is not a policy, it is an inconsistency: if rolling over were the intent,
month 13 would roll over into next January too. A day that does not exist in
the month it names is an `Err`, and the century rule is applied, so
`1900-02-29` is refused and `2000-02-29` is not.

### `std/path`

Paths as text, with **one separator**. A path is written with `/` and read with
either, so a Windows path pasted into a program works and a path this module
produces looks the same everywhere. Node's own `path` changes behaviour with
the platform, which would make the same Lumen program print different things on
different machines — the same reason `std/time` has only UTC. A drive letter
(`C:`) and a UNC root (`//server/share`) are understood and preserved, because
losing one silently turns an absolute path into a relative one and a program
that then writes a file writes it somewhere else.

Nothing here touches the filesystem — `exists` lives in `std/fs`, because it
asks the machine a question — which is what lets a program work out where things
will go before doing any of it.

`isInside(parent, child)` is the check a program serving files needs, with both
ways of getting it wrong already handled: comparing text alone makes
`/publicity` look like it is inside `/public`, and forgetting to normalise lets
`/public/../etc/passwd` through.

### `std/regex`

A pattern is a `Str`. There is no `/.../` literal, deliberately: it would be
ambiguous with division in a language whose newlines are significant, and every
escape a pattern needs would then have to be understood by the lexer as well as
by the matcher. A string keeps the whole question in one place — and `"\\d+"`
is what other languages write inside a string anyway.

**The dialect is ECMAScript**, because the host's engine is. `\d`, `\w`, `\s`,
`\b`, groups, named groups `(?<name>…)`, alternation, greedy and lazy
quantifiers, lookahead, lookbehind and character classes all mean what they mean
in JavaScript, Java, Python and everything else descended from Perl.

Every function that takes a pattern returns a `Result`, because a pattern comes
from somewhere — a config file, an argument, a person — and `(` is an ordinary
thing to type. `isValid` is the exception: asking whether something is a pattern
cannot itself fail.

A match is a map with `text`, `at`, `groups` and `named`. A group that did not
take part is `nil` rather than missing, so the list is the same length whichever
branch of an alternation fired.

`at` is a **code point** index, the same unit `std/str.slice`, `len` and `chars`
use — so a match can be recovered from its own position, which is the one thing
the field is for:

```lumen
match find(text, "\\d+").unwrapOr(None) {
  Some(m) => slice(text, m.at, m.at + len(m.text)),   // == m.text, always
  None    => "",
}
```

The engine reports UTF-16 offsets, and those are converted. Handing the engine's
number straight back made `at` point one place past the match for every astral
character before it.

Three named options rather than a flags string, because `multiline: true` says
what it does and `"gm"` is a thing to look up — and because `help()` then lists
them:

| Option | What it changes |
|---|---|
| `ignoreCase` | `a` matches `A` |
| `multiline` | `^` and `$` match at every line, not only the ends of the text |
| `dotAll` | `.` matches a newline too |

`(?m)` is **not** the way to ask for the second: JavaScript has no inline
modifier group, so a pattern written that way does not compile — and gets an
`Err` saying so rather than quietly matching nothing.

There is no `unicode` option. It would reject patterns that work in every other
tool — a bare `\d` inside a class, a lone `{` — and a valid pattern being
refused here is a worse surprise than `.` matching half an astral character.

**There is no backtracking guard.** `(a+)+b` against a long run of `a`s takes
time exponential in its length, here as in most engines, and nothing interrupts
it: thirty characters is already a program that does not come back.

**Both sides are the hazard, not just the pattern.** A pattern from a stranger
is the obvious half. The half that actually bites is a pattern *you* wrote,
applied to text somebody else chose — a hard-coded validator against a submitted
field is the classic shape, and "my patterns are all literals" is not the
defence it sounds like. Either side being untrusted is enough.

What to do about it: prefer `std/str` — `contains`, `startsWith`, `splitOnce`,
`count` — which cannot backtrack at all, and keep a quantifier from containing
another (`(a+)+`, `(a|a)*`, `(.*)*`) when a pattern must meet input from
outside. Bounding the input's length first is the other half, since the blow-up
is in *its* length rather than the pattern's.

`std/web`'s router does not use this module: a route pattern is matched by
splitting the path into segments and comparing them, so no request can make a
server backtrack. That is a property worth keeping, and a test holds it.

### `std/process`

**There is no shell.** A command is a name and a list of arguments, never one
string for `/bin/sh` to take apart. That is a design rather than a precaution:
with a shell, every call has to decide how to quote whatever it interpolates,
and the one that forgets turns a file called `; rm -rf ~` into a disaster. With
an argument list there is nothing to quote, because nothing is ever parsed.

What that gives up is worth naming plainly:

| Instead of | Write |
|---|---|
| `ls *.txt` | `walk(dir)` from `std/fs`, then `filter` |
| `a \| b` | run `a`, then run `b` with its output as `input` |
| `a > out.txt` | take `out` and `write` it |
| `a && b` | run `a`, then run `b` if `ok` |

Each is a line of Lumen instead, which is a fair price for never thinking about
quoting again — and every one of them is clearer written out.

**Nothing raises.** A command that does not exist, one that fails, and one that
takes too long are all `Result`s. A non-zero `status` is `Ok`, because "did this
program work" is the question the caller is asking and `grep` says "no match"
that way; `Err` is reserved for not having run at all. `timedOut` is its own
field rather than a status to interpret, because a timeout and a failure want
different handling.

`timeout` of zero waits forever, which is what a build wants and exactly what
something a stranger's input chose does not. A *negative* timeout is an `Err`
rather than a longer wait: it is what `deadline - now()` gives once the deadline
has passed, and a caller who has run out of time wants anything but no limit.

`Err` names the thing that was actually wrong. A missing `cwd` says so — `cannot
run \`pwd\` in \`/tmp/gone\`: no such directory` — rather than blaming the program,
which is what the host's own error would do: Node reports a missing directory
with exactly the `ENOENT` it reports for a missing program, so this module looks
at the directory before it spawns in order to be able to tell you which.

### Randomness

`random()` and `randomInt(low, high)` draw from the host by default, so a
program is different on every run — which is what you want, and the opposite of
what a test wants.

`seed(n)` replaces the generator with one written here, so the same seed gives
the same sequence on every machine and every version of Node. That is what makes
a randomised test repeatable when it fails, which is most of what randomised
tests are for. `shuffle` uses Fisher-Yates, which is uniform; the spelling
everybody reaches for first — `sortBy(fn(_) { random() })` — is not, because a
comparison sort asks about the same pair more than once and gets different
answers each time.

**Not cryptographic.** `seed` is for repeatability, not for secrets.
